text.p: The following is a direct contribution from commodity statistician F.O. Licht in Ratzeburg, Germany. Please address any queries to Helmut Ahlfeld on +00 49 4541 88920.

Robusta futures in London stayed in a tight range in the afternoon trade after a relatively quiet New York session and prices ended the day with pared gains. The market moved higher at the start on short-covering buying but Indonesian origin offers knocked it back from the peaks. Benchmark May gave up further gains by the close, settling just $5 higher at $1,615 a tonne while July firmed $13 at $1,643 a tonne. May/July switches were again active as funds rolled forward their May positions.

Analysts said the technical picture could improve if May clears above $1,668, the April 2 high. But it could struggle to regain a foothold at the recent peak of just above $1,800. Arabica futures in New York ended higher again on Thursday on moderate volume, but the two nearby contracts traded inside Wednesday's range, after the spot May contract climbed to new contract highs on April 16. CSCE May coffee ended up 1.75 cents/lb at 209.80 cents/lb, after trading a 206.10-211.50 intraday range. The May contract is approaching first notice day on April 22, while the July contract now has more open interest. CSCE July coffee ended up 2.20 cents/lb at 187.50 cents/lb. The outer months closed down 5.50 cents/lb to up 1.75 cents/lb.

COLOMBIA - Transportation Minister Carlos Hernan Lopez said the Colombian government may move to outlaw strike by truck drivers set to begin at midnight Saturday. Lopez said the government has already complied with 85 per cent of the drivers' demands and therefore the strike has all the characteristics of being declared illegal. He said military measures of a preventive type would be used to guarantee the transportation of cargo and passengers if the work stoppage by the Colombian Truck Drivers' Association ACC goes forward as planned. In his remarks, Lopez also raised fears that leftist guerrillas would somehow seek to take advantage of the strike and add to Colombia's pressing political problems.

EL SALVADOR - El Salvador exported 1.710 mn 60-kg bags of coffee through April 10, Salvadorean Coffee Council economic analyst Tomas Bonilla said. The country had sold about 76 per cent of its exportable coffee output for about $260 mn as of April 10, he told Reuters. He said the country still has about 450,000 bags of coffee to export for the 1996/97 coffee season. El Salvador had exportable coffee for the season of 2.25 to 2.45 mn bags.

SPAIN - Coffee imports in November 1996 amounted to 325,343 60-kg bags, up from 270,494 bags in November 1995. This brought cumulative imports in the first eleven months of 1996 (January/November) up to 3.343 mn bags, up more than 11 per cent on the volume imported in the corresponding period one year ago. Total imports in 1995 amounted to 3.225 mn bags against 3.155 mn bags in 1994. Major suppliers of green coffee in January/November 1996 were Uganda (892,400 vs 595,800 bags), Brazil (339,700 vs 544,800 bags), Colombia (335,400 vs 291,400 bags) and Vietnam (162,100 vs 200,600 bags). Coffee exports in November 1996 reached 86,361 bags, up from 31,396 bags in November 1995. This brought cumulative exports in 1996 up to 534,836 bags, a plus of almost 48 per cent compared to the volume exported in 1995. Total exports in 1995 reached 400,986 bags against 429,924 bags in 1994.
